title: Cumulative frequency and percentiles
log: 2026-11-01T14:46:39Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: None of the bank points teaches running totals of frequencies or percentiles from data; the closest, the cumulative distribution function, is a calculus idea about density curves at a different depth, so a new point is needed.

draft.title: Cumulative frequency and percentiles
card: Cumulative frequency is a running total. For each value or class, add its frequency to all the frequencies before it. The last total equals the number of values.
Example: Frequencies of 4, 6, 10 and 5 give cumulative frequencies of 4, 10, 20 and 25. So 20 of the 25 values are in the first three classes.
A percentile shows where a value sits. The 40th percentile is the value with about 40% of the data at or below it.
To find a percentile, work out that percentage of the total count, then read across to the value. In 25 values, the 40th percentile is near the 10th value, as 0.4 × 25 = 10.
draft.remember: Cumulative frequency counts values up to a point. A percentile turns that count into a percentage.

a.q: Frequencies for four classes are 3, 7, 12 and 8. What are the cumulative frequencies?
a.why: Add each frequency to the running total: 3, 3 + 7 = 10, 10 + 12 = 22, 22 + 8 = 30. The last total must equal the number of values. Repeating the frequencies adds nothing up.
a.clue: Each total includes every class before it.

b.q: A school records 80 swim times. Tia's time has 60 times at or below it. What is her percentile?
b.why: The percentile is 60 ÷ 80 × 100 = 75. So 75% of times are at or below hers. Using 60 itself ignores that the total is 80, not 100.
b.clue: Divide the count at or below by the total count.
